overview: Two regulatory DNA sequences in an operon, one where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription and the other where a repressor can block it.
genZNote: Promoter: where RNA polymerase parks and gets ready to go. Operator: the checkpoint gate that a repressor can slam shut.

aspects.label: Function
aspects.valueA: The site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription.
aspects.valueB: The site where a repressor protein binds to block transcription.

aspects.label: Position Relative to Genes
aspects.valueA: Located upstream of the structural genes, before the operator.
aspects.valueB: Located between the promoter and the structural genes.

aspects.label: Bound By
aspects.valueA: Bound by RNA polymerase (and sigma factor in bacteria).
aspects.valueB: Bound by a repressor protein (or sometimes an activator, depending on the system).

overlay.examHighYieldNote: In the lac operon, when lactose is absent, the repressor binds the operator and physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes, even though the promoter is right next door.
overlay.memoryTrick: Promoter = 'come on in', RNA polymerase's landing spot. Operator = the gate a repressor can lock.
overlay.commonMisconception: The operator is not the same site as the promoter — they are adjacent but distinct sequences with opposite regulatory roles (enabling versus blocking transcription).
